front: Boy, 6 months, runny nose for 2 days, respiratory stridor, temp 101F. Most likely location of the pathology?

items.a: The larynx. Diagnosis is laryngotracheobronchitis (croup) caused by parainfluenza virus, with a classic seal-like, barking cough.

front: Infant, 10 months, fever 101F, bilateral wheezes. Diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: "Community-acquired viral infection," i.e. RSV bronchiolitis. Treatment is supportive; ribavirin and palivizumab are almost always wrong.

front: 8M, recent URTI, now stridor and fever 101F. Diagnosis, organism, diagnosis method and treatment?

items.a: Bacterial tracheitis, usually S. aureus. Diagnose with bronchoscopy. Treat with a third-generation cephalosporin plus an aminopenicillin (for example IV flucloxacillin).

front: 3F, 2-week cough and congestion, loud snoring for 6 months, mouth breathing, 1/6 holosystolic murmur, loud S2, cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary vascular markings, echo with RV hypertrophy and mild TR. Long-term management?

items.a: Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy. Chronic upper airway obstruction can cause obstructive lung disease with cor pulmonale; the loud S2 and increased vascular markings suggest pulmonary hypertension, and TR can be seen in pulmonary HTN.

front: 5F, pale conjunctivae, low Hb, low MCV, normal WBC and platelets, low RDW. Diagnosis and next step?

items.a: Decreased synthesis of globin chains (thalassemia). Target cells on the smear are a giveaway. Next best step: hemoglobin electrophoresis. Thalassemia has a low RDW (uniformly small RBCs), whereas IDA has a high RDW.

front: 4M, itchy head, small oval areas of alopecia on the scalp. Organism and treatment?

items.a: Trichophyton tonsurans: tinea capitis. Treat the patient with oral griseofulvin; reduce risk by not sharing hats (three questions on the peds forms).

front: 14F with Down syndrome, polycythemia, moderate cyanosis, clubbing, no murmur but loud S2, echo with large VSD and dilated main pulmonary artery. Mechanism for the polycythemia?

items.a: Pulmonary artery hypertension (Peds NBME). Diagnosis is Eisenmenger syndrome: a large VSD with reversal to R to L shunting. Large VSDs may present without a murmur.

front: Neonate under 34 weeks with dyspnea. Diagnosis and the L/S ratio?

items.a: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS; hyaline membrane disease). A healthy lecithin (dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine) to sphingomyelin ratio is above 2; the ratio is reduced in NRDS.

front: 8M with sore throat and a new-onset tic. Diagnosis and next step?

items.a: PANDAS (Pediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorder Associated with Streptococcus). Group A Strep can precipitate OCD, Tourette and ADHD. Answer: check streptolysin O titers. High-yield for Psych shelf, Peds shelf and 2CK.

front: 11-month-old boy, red tongue, maculopapular body rash, fever 100.5F. Diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: Scarlet fever (Group A Strep). Give penicillin to prevent rheumatic fever. The tongue is called strawberry.

front: 17F with an itchy maculopapular back rash and a pink 2-cm ellipse on the lower back. Next step?

items.a: Reassurance and observation. Diagnosis: pityriasis rosea, caused by HHV-6 and HHV-7; self-limiting, lasting 5 weeks on average.

front: 6F with axillary and groin freckling and a small growth in the eye seen by her mother. Diagnosis and features?

items.a: Neurofibromatosis type I (NF1): Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), optic glioma, axillary and groin freckling, neurofibromas (cutaneous lumps), cafe au lait spots (hyperpigmented macules), pheochromocytoma.

front: 3F with 2 weeks of fever, pallor, poor appetite, mouth ulcers and low RBCs, WBCs and platelets. Diagnosis and next step?

items.a: Aplastic anemia (presumably from Parvo, but also other viruses). Next best step: immediate IV antibiotics for neutropenic fever. Low WBCs means low neutrophils, and mouth ulcers on USMLE are a hugely HY presentation of neutropenia.

front: 3F with fever and low RBCs, WBCs and platelets, already on IV antibiotics. Next best step in diagnosis?

items.a: Bone marrow aspiration (sounds invasive, but it diagnoses aplastic anemia). A UWorld question with Parvo IgM/IgG titers is for an adult daycare worker with a lacy body rash and no drop in blood cell lines.

front: 6M with recurrent Staph infections and diarrhea. Diagnosis and mechanism?

items.a: "Neutrophil oxidative burst" defect: chronic granulomatous disease (NADPH oxidase deficiency), with infections by catalase-positive organisms (Staph infections are the signature complication).

front: 17M with 12 months of intermittent swelling of the face and lips, chest and arms, with abdominal pain and diarrhea during episodes. Next best step in diagnosis?

items.a: Measurement of C1 esterase inhibitor concentration (not C1 esterase). Diagnosis: hereditary angioedema.

front: 2-month-old boy with non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting after feeds, increasing in amount and force. Diagnosis and associations?

items.a: Pyloric stenosis. Associated with first-born males and oral erythromycin use (a motilin receptor agonist; also treats chlamydia ophthalmia neonatorum).

front: 2-month-old boy with bilious vomiting and Down syndrome. Diagnosis and imaging?

items.a: Duodenal atresia. AXR shows the double bubble sign. Mechanism: "failure of canalization of proximal bowel." Annular pancreas can be an alternative cause of bilious vomiting plus double bubble (not with Down syndrome).

front: 18-month-old girl with 24 hours of intermittent abdominal pain, an RLQ mass and a positive fecal occult blood test. Next best step in diagnosis?

items.a: Air-contrast enema (or contrast, or air). Ultrasound (target sign) may be done, but on the NBME the answer for diagnosing intussusception is always enema (diagnostic and therapeutic). Presentation is almost always under 2 years with an intermittent nature (the sentence continues on p169).

front: 3F with failure to thrive, 3 months of steatorrhea, and no meconium passage until day 3. Mechanism for failure to thrive?

items.a: "Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency." The Peds shelf frequently refers to cystic fibrosis this way (it can also refer to chronic pancreatitis in adults).

front: 3-month-old boy with fever, pyuria and few bacteria. Next best step in diagnosis?

items.a: Renal ultrasound. Most likely pyelonephritis (few bacteria are typical on UA despite pyuria). Do renal and bladder ultrasound for all kids aged 2-24 months with a febrile UTI, to screen for congenital GU tract abnormalities.

front: Neonatal male with posterior urethral valves. Next best step in diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: Voiding cystourethrogram. Treatment must be surgery.

front: 34M falls on a balance beam (saddle injury) with blood at the urethral meatus. Diagnosis and next best step?

items.a: Urethral injury; do a retrograde urethrogram.

front: 16M skiing accident with bruising and/or flank pain and red urine. Diagnosis and next best step?

items.a: Kidney injury (renal contusion); do CT with contrast, not ultrasound. Exceedingly HY on surgery forms; it sounds wrong because contrast can be nephrotoxic, but the exams still want CT with contrast.

front: Kid with bloody diarrhea, petechiae and red urine. Diagnosis and mechanism?

items.a: Hemolytic uremic syndrome from EHEC O157:H7 or Shigella. Triad: thrombocytopenia, schistocytosis (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia) and renal insufficiency. Per the source, toxin inhibits ADAMTS13 in afferent arterioles and damages endothelium, causing platelet consumption and clumping; RBCs shear on the clumps.

front: 12M with epistaxis, bleeding time 9 minutes and platelet count 50,000. Diagnosis and mechanism?

items.a: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP); antibodies against GpIIb/IIIa following a viral infection (2CK questions often omit the preceding viral illness).

front: 5M with hemarthrosis. Diagnosis until proven otherwise, and key facts?

items.a: Hemophilia A or B (choose A if both are listed and you cannot tell them apart; A is far more common). Both X-linked recessive with isolated aPTT increase; A is factor VIII deficiency, B (Christmas disease) is factor IX deficiency. Hemarthrosis is classic for hemophilia but rare in vWD.

front: 12M with epistaxis, bleeding time 9 minutes and platelets 50,000. Most effective way to decrease recurrence?

items.a: Splenectomy. Steroids come first, but splenectomy is still the most effective at decreasing recurrence.

front: 3F with a viral infection, fever and a tonic-clonic seizure. Diagnosis, risk and treatment?

items.a: Febrile seizure. Fever can precipitate seizures in 2-4% of children aged 6 months to 5 years; about a two-fold progression to epilepsy versus the general population; treatment is a benzodiazepine.

front: 8M with bloating and flatulence after dairy products. Next best step in diagnosis?

items.a: Hydrogen breath test, or testing for decreased stool pH; diagnosis is lactose intolerance.

front: 2F with iron deficiency anemia, bloating, diarrhea, and now eating table food. Diagnosis and workup?

items.a: Celiac disease (can cause iron deficiency anemia); diagnose with antibody screen: anti-endomysial, anti-gliadin, or anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA.

front: 5F with a positive celiac antibody screen. Next best step (duodenal biopsy vs no further studies)?

items.a: Duodenal biopsy (flattened villi); it sounds wrong, but it is what the NBME wants.

front: Treatment for an infant with milk or soy protein allergy on USMLE?

items.a: Switch to hydrolyzed formula (proteins processed into fragments); the FDA labels hydrolyzed formulas as hypoallergenic. The page then starts listing types of milk protein allergy, beginning with FPIES (continues on p176).

front: 3F who finished a 10-day antibiotic course, now with fever 101F, LLQ tenderness and positive fecal occult blood. Diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: C. difficile; treat with vancomycin. Two points: C. diff frequently causes bloody stool on 2CK forms; and the pseudoappendicitis of Y. enterocolitica is truly RLQ (terminal ileitis or mesenteric adenitis), not LLQ.

front: 16-month-old with Giardia infection and failure to thrive. Mechanism of failure to thrive and treatment?

items.a: Malabsorption of fats and carbohydrates; treat Giardia with metronidazole.

front: 16M with acutely painful testes and a negative cremasteric reflex. Diagnosis and workup?

items.a: Testicular torsion; Doppler ultrasound followed by surgical detorsion.

front: 6M with a painful testis with blue/black discoloration of the superior pole, decreased bowel sounds, and a rigid abdomen. Diagnosis and management?

items.a: Strangulated hernia, not testicular torsion; operative management.

front: 14M with heaviness or bogginess of the testes. Diagnosis and management?

items.a: Varicocele (one FM shelf question literally says bag of worms). Diagnose with Doppler ultrasound; elective surgery may reduce the risk of sub-fertility from increased testicular temperature.

front: 3M with large calves who uses his arms to crawl up off the floor. Mechanism and diagnosis?

items.a: Defective cytoskeletal connection to the extracellular matrix; Duchenne muscular dystrophy (X-linked recessive), caused by a frameshift mutation. Becker is less severe, presents in adolescence or early adulthood, and is not a frameshift (e.g. missense).

front: 14F with 10 months of tripping, high-arched feet, hammer toes, hand and foot muscle wasting, absent ankle reflexes, reduced vibration and proprioception in the legs, and prolonged distal motor latencies. Diagnosis and mechanism?

items.a: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy); defective protein production for myelin sheaths and nerve fibers; hammer toes classic; pes cavus also seen.

front: 10F with violaceous erythema of the upper eyelids and scaly knuckles and finger joints. Diagnosis and workup?

items.a: Dermatomyositis (asked on Peds NBME): heliotrope rash and mechanic's hands; Gottron papules and shawl rash can also be seen. Workup with EMG and anti-Jo1/anti-Mi2 (same as polymyositis); definitive diagnosis is muscle biopsy; treat acute flares with steroids.

front: 6M with suspected JRA and a red, hot, painful knee. Next step?

items.a: Arthrocentesis to rule out septic arthritis. If the vignette sounds like classic transient synovitis (hip, not knee), arthrocentesis is not needed.

front: 4M with increased bilirubin after a viral infection or drug, and degmacytes (bite cells) on smear. Mechanism and diagnosis?

items.a: Decreased NADPH production; G6PD deficiency (X-linked recessive). Bite cells are degmacytes; Heinz bodies (denatured, oxidized Hb) are also seen in RBCs.

front: Kid with suspected JRA and a sore knee. Next step?

items.a: Arthrocentesis to rule out septic arthritis.

front: 9F with both legs bowed, a small child and/or a malabsorptive disease (Crohn, CF). Diagnosis and labs?

items.a: Rickets (vitamin D deficiency); also low calcium, low phosphate, high PTH and high ALP (because PTH is high).

front: 4-month-old with clicking/clunking on exam, positive Ortolani and Barlow maneuvers. Diagnosis and next steps?

items.a: Primary hip dysplasia (congenital hip dysplasia). Once positive, the next best step is ortho referral if listed (always sounds wrong but is correct); if not listed, do ultrasound under 6 months or x-ray over 6 months. Treat with an abduction harness (Pavlik harness; frog-leg-like).

front: 11-13-year-old overweight boy with a painful limp. Diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: SCFE; treatment is surgical pinning.

front: Kid falls on an outstretched arm with pain over the anatomical snuffbox. Diagnosis and next step?

items.a: Scaphoid fracture; do an x-ray.

front: 17F with BMI 33 and irregular periods. Diagnosis and mechanism?

items.a: Anovulation: insulin resistance leads to abnormal GnRH pulsation, high LH/FSH, and insufficient FSH, so the follicle is not primed when the LH spike arrives and is retained as a cyst. With hirsutism the diagnosis is PCOS (the source says 11 cysts bilaterally per Amsterdam criteria). On Peds form 5 the location of pathology in PCOS is the ovary, not the hypothalamus.

front: 10F with polyuria and polydipsia and a sore throat two weeks earlier. Most likely infective diagnosis?

items.a: Coxsackie B virus; it can precipitate type 1 diabetes through molecular mimicry (the bullet continues about antibodies on p183).

front: 6M with nocturnal enuresis. Next best step, in the order the exams want,?

items.a: Behavioral answer first (spend more time with the child, reduce stressors); if not an answer, star chart (positive reinforcement); if not listed or already tried, enuresis alarm. Medications like imipramine and desmopressin are always wrong, as is water deprivation after 5 pm.

front: 16-17-year-old who has been going on dates recently with a sore throat. Diagnosis and test?

items.a: EBV mononucleosis; do a heterophile antibody test (Monospot).

front: 9-month-old boy with 5 days of fever, edema of the dorsa of the hands, cervical lymphadenopathy, cracked lips, and red oral mucosa and conjunctivae. Treatment and diagnosis?

items.a: High-dose aspirin plus IVIG; Kawasaki disease. Never give aspirin to a kid (Reye syndrome) unless the diagnosis is Kawasaki; other features are palm and sole desquamation and coronary artery aneurysms.

front: 8M with a non-productive cough worse at night, shortness of breath during the day, and mild hyperinflation on CXR. Next best step in diagnosis?

items.a: Spirometry (answer on NBME); diagnosis is asthma.

front: 16M with a large red, non-vesicular rash on the chin; the question asks for a diagnosis based on an image. Answer?

items.a: Impetigo (do not chase HSV or tinea faciei).

front: 8M with an ear infection one month ago, slightly reduced hearing in one ear, fluid behind the tympanic membrane, afebrile and well-appearing. Diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: Otitis media with effusion (serous otitis media): fluid occasionally persists after OM resolves (it need not be recurrent OM); treat with observation, as it usually self-resolves in 4-8 weeks.

front: 7M with squamous proliferation seen behind the tympanic membrane. Diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: Cholesteatoma; it gradually grows and invades the inner ear, causing irreversible hearing loss; treatment is surgical excision.

front: 10F with a sore throat two weeks ago, red urine, peripheral edema and hypertension. Mechanism of the hypertension?

items.a: Volume overload: microvascular disturbance from the glomerulonephritis with RAAS stimulation.

front: 17F with hypertension, low K and high bicarbonate. Next best step and diagnosis?

items.a: MR angiogram of the renal arteries; diagnosis is fibromuscular dysplasia (another answer: increased renin production).

front: 15M with a unilateral mass behind the nipple with or without tenderness. Answer?

items.a: Reassurance; physiologic gynecomastia of puberty (higher androgens are aromatized to estrogens).

front: 17F with very bad period pain that makes her miss class sometimes, and a normal physical exam. Diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: Primary dysmenorrhea from prostaglandin hypersecretion (PGF2alpha); give NSAIDs.

front: 14F who never had a period, with 1 week of constant severe pelvic pain, 6 months of intermittent pelvic pain, BP 90/50 and a bluish bulge in the upper vagina. Diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: Hematometra: imperforate hymen with blood collection in the uterus; vagal response causes low BP; treatment is cruciate incision of the hymen.

front: 14F who never had a period, with 6 months of intermittent pelvic pain, normal BP and a bluish bulge in the upper vagina. Diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: Hematocolpos: blood collection in the vaginal canal, not backed up to the uterus like hematometra; treatment is cruciate incision of the hymen.

front: 16F with a vagina ending in a blind pouch, no cervix or uterus, absent or scanty pubic and axillary hair, and Tanner stage 4. Diagnosis and next step?

items.a: Androgen insensitivity syndrome; next step is karyotyping (46,XY).

front: 16F with a vagina ending in a blind pouch, no cervix or uterus, coarse pubic and axillary hair, and Tanner stage 4. Diagnosis and next step?

items.a: Mullerian agenesis; next step is karyotyping (46,XX).

front: 3M with a painless flank mass and no other information. Diagnosis and next step?

items.a: Wilms tumor; the answer on the Peds form is ultrasonography of the abdomen.

front: 4F with her third pyelonephritis and a high creatinine. Most likely cause and pathology?

items.a: Congenital urinary tract obstruction or vesicoureteral reflux; chronic pyelonephritis from recurrent acute pyelonephritis, with thyroidization of the kidney and blunting and scarring of the renal calyces.

front: 5M with 4 days of increasing shortness of breath, a superior mediastinal mass on CXR and thoracentesis giving 400 mL serosanguinous fluid. Most likely cause of the effusion?

items.a: Malignant pleural effusion from T-cell ALL (the mediastinal mass causes an SVC-like syndrome).

front: Neonate with total bilirubin 14 mg/dL and direct bilirubin 13 mg/dL. Diagnosis, next step and treatment?

items.a: Biliary atresia; next step is liver biopsy; treatment is liver transplant. Total bilirubin is okay here, but direct is severely pathologic because it is above 10% of total (over 1.4 mg/dL).

front: Neonate with total bilirubin 20 mg/dL, all unconjugated, continually worsening despite management. Diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: Crigler-Najjar: absence of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase; treatment is liver transplant. Type II is a deficiency, not absence, of the enzyme and can be managed with phenobarbital, which reduces bilirubin.

front: Pathologic jaundice in a neonate, mom O+, neonate A or B blood type. Diagnosis and mechanism?

items.a: Hemolytic disease of the newborn (ABO type): mothers with O blood type have a fraction of IgG (rather than all IgM) against A and B antigens, which crosses the placenta and causes fetal hemolysis; severity is highly variable.

front: Neonate with low potassium, low glucose and low DHEA-S. Diagnosis (the source explanation continues in the source)?

items.a: CAH due to 17-hydroxylase deficiency; potassium wasting from high mineralocorticoid activity.

front: 7F with progressive fatigue over 6 months, low BP and darkening of skin. Most effective test to determine diagnosis and management (Peds NBME)? Diagnosis?

items.a: Plasma cortisol; diagnosis is Addison disease.

front: Neonate with diffuse pink body rash and desquamation of palms and soles. Mechanism and diagnosis?

items.a: Exotoxin; staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome due to exfoliative toxin (produced by about 5% of community staph).

front: Neonate born at home, umbilical cord cut with a kitchen knife and tied with twine, with trismus. Diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: Tetanus; Tx = antitoxin. Trismus is lockjaw (do not confuse with tenesmus, the intractable feeling of needing to defecate). C. tetani classically enters through the umbilical stump.

front: Neonate born at home with bleeding from the umbilical stump. Diagnosis and BT, PT, aPTT?

items.a: Vitamin K deficiency; bleeding time normal, PT and aPTT both elevated; due to a sterile bowel and no injection at birth.

front: Neonate with intracranial calcifications, deafness, with or without hepatosplenomegaly and blueberry muffin rash. Diagnosis and reasoning?

items.a: Congenital CMV. Calcifications are non-specific but the triad is not for toxoplasmosis; deafness is very high yield for CMV although not specific; diagnose CMV by eliminating toxo, syphilis, rubella and varicella descriptions.

front: 16F sexually active. Pap smears and/or STI checks?

items.a: Do not do Pap smears; start at age 21 regardless of age of onset of sexual activity. Do check for chlamydia and gonorrhea starting from the age of sexual onset, and make sure she has had the HPV vaccine.

front: 16F with mucopurulent discharge and adnexal pain. Treatment and diagnosis?

items.a: Pelvic inflammatory disease; IM ceftriaxone PLUS either oral azithromycin (one stat dose) or oral doxycycline (BID for a week); always cotreat for chlamydia and gonorrhea; if the patient is septic give IV antibiotics.

front: 17F asymptomatic, male partner recently tested positive for gonorrhea; tests ordered. Treat or not?

items.a: Treat: IM ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline. The wrong answer is no treatment because she is asymptomatic.

front: 16M with redness of both eyes, rash over extremities and mucopurulent urethral discharge. Diagnosis and cause?

items.a: Reactive arthritis due to chlamydia; gonococcus does not cause reactive arthritis.

front: 16M with polyarthritis, positive Finkelstein test and cutaneous papules over the wrist. Diagnosis and presentations?

items.a: Gonococcal arthritis; it presents either as a monoarthritis of a large joint such as the knee, or as a triad of polyarthritis, tenosynovitis and cutaneous papules.

front: 16F with thin, grey, watery discharge, diagnosed by wet mount. Diagnosis, findings and treatment?

items.a: Bacterial vaginosis (Gardnerella); clue cells (squamous cells covered in bacteria) on wet mount; KOH whiff test with fishy odor is also classic; treat with topical metronidazole gel.

front: 16F with yellow-green discharge, diagnosed by wet mount. Diagnosis, findings and treatment?

items.a: Trichomonas vaginalis; wet mount shows flagellated protozoa; strawberry cervix (punctate hemorrhages) or an erythematous vaginal canal might be seen; treat with topical metronidazole for patient and partner (high risk of reinfection).

front: 17M back from Uganda with a painful crater at the base of the penile shaft. Diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid); treat with azithromycin.

front: 17F, BMI 28, erythematous and itchy vulva, no mention of discharge but the question asks for the organism. Diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: Candidiasis; classically curd-like white discharge, but one 2CK-level question does not mention it. Treat with topical nystatin first or oral fluconazole (topical nystatin usually tried first).

front: 4M with bitemporal hemianopsia and calcification on MRI. Diagnosis and facts?

items.a: Craniopharyngioma; the most common pituitary-region tumor in peds (prolactinoma in adults), though some sources say it is not a true pituitary tumor since it derives from Rathke pouch (roof of primitive pharynx). It can calcify, has motor-oil appearance, and frequently recurs after surgery.

front: 6M in whom the image shows the eye looking like it was hit by a softball. Diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: Orbital cellulitis; must give IV antibiotics. In contrast, pre-septal cellulitis is less severe and can be treated with oral antibiotics.

front: 6M with a painful bump on the eyelid. Diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: Hordeolum (stye); S. aureus infection; treat with warm compresses.

front: 6M with a painless bump on the eyelid. Diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: Chalazion (blocked oil duct); treat with warm compresses.

front: 6M with IQ of 60, small for age, born to a mother aged 41, no other information. Most likely cause of intellectual disability?

items.a: Down syndrome, not FAS. FAS is the most common cause overall, but if the question wants FAS it mentions the philtrum, and the source says Down syndrome is the most common cause of intellectual disability when the mother is over 40.

front: 8M with prominent jaw, protruding ears and IQ of 65. Most likely explanation?

items.a: A fragile site on the X chromosome: Fragile X (CGG trinucleotide repeat disorder).

front: 2M with blisters on the tongue and mouth. Next best step and diagnosis?

items.a: Fiberoptic endoscopy; diagnosis is exposure to drain cleaner.

front: 16F with long history of depression on a new medication, large pupils, dry skin and QT changes on ECG. Treatment and mechanism?

items.a: Sodium bicarbonate; treatment for TCA toxicity. It causes dissociation of the TCA from myocardial sodium channels. TCA is basic, not acidic (in contrast to salicylates), so bicarb actually decreases urinary excretion, but the mechanism as an antidote is different. TCAs cause CCC: coma, convulsions, cardiotoxicity, plus anticholinergic, anti-alpha-1-adrenergic and anti-H1-histaminergic side effects.

front: Pregnant woman with new dyspnea in the 2nd trimester and a diastolic murmur?

items.a: Mitral stenosis becomes symptomatic from the 50% rise in plasma volume by the 2nd trimester. Do not confuse with severe dyspnea and edema in the late third trimester, which is peripartum cardiomyopathy (antibody-mediated).

front: Open PDA masking cyanosis, and a week-old cyanotic baby with normal APGARs?

items.a: An open PDA can mask cyanosis in conditions such as hypoplastic left heart syndrome or pre-ductal coarctation. A kid with normal APGARs who becomes cyanotic a week later: closure of the ductus arteriosus.

front: Post-term neonate (42-43 weeks) with meconium-stained fluid and an echo showing R to L shunt across the foramen ovale?

items.a: Persistent fetal circulation (persistent pulmonary hypertension): the answer is failure of pulmonary vasodilation. Meconium aspiration can decrease opening of the lung vasculature, increasing right heart pressure and risk.

front: Stroke, TIA or retinal artery occlusion in a hypertensive patient?

items.a: A plaque from one of the carotids has launched off; HTN increases risk.
A plaque from one of the carotids has launched off; HTN increases risk.

front: Patient after a motor vehicle accident with widening of the mediastinum, next best step?

items.a: Aortic angiography (aortography) OR CT angiography. A new 2CK form has 'CT scan of the chest' as the answer, meaning CT angiography. NBME/USMLE will not force a choice between aortography and CTA.

front: Labetalol in a patient with low BP from rupture or dissection?

items.a: Still the NBME answer: the drug decreases shearing forces, even with low BP. Do not reject it because of low BP.

front: Perioperative MI risk in a 6-cm AAA patient?

items.a: Assess with a pre-op stress test. 2CK NBME Q: dipyridamole and thallium pharmacologic stress test.
Assess with a pre-op stress test. 2CK NBME Q: dipyridamole and thallium pharmacologic stress test.

front: Pulsatile hematoma in the neck of a trauma patient?

items.a: 2CK loves this; the answer is endotracheal intubation.
2CK loves this; the answer is endotracheal intubation.

front: 45-year-old man with nosebleeds since adolescence, S3 and dyspnea, with a tongue picture (NBME): cause of dyspnea?

items.a: Pulmonary arteriovenous fistula, leading to high-output failure; the diagnosis is hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. USMLE almost always shows red dots on the tongue/mouth or finger in a patient with nosebleeds.

front: 75-year-old with a TIA, normal BP and a sinus-rhythm ECG: next best step?

items.a: Holter monitor (24-hour ambulatory ECG) to pick up paroxysmal AF, which comes and goes.
Holter monitor (24-hour ambulatory ECG) to pick up paroxysmal AF, which comes and goes.

front: Severe leg pain with absent pulses in a patient with irregularly irregular rhythm?

items.a: Acute limb ischemia (embolus from AF); USMLE wants embolectomy.
Acute limb ischemia (embolus from AF); USMLE wants embolectomy.

front: Stroke-like presentation in a patient with MI weeks ago?

items.a: Embolus from ventricular septal aneurysm (on a 2CK form).
Embolus from ventricular septal aneurysm (on a 2CK form).

front: 22-year-old man with chest pain after heavy partying and diffuse ST elevations?

items.a: Cocaine-related pericarditis.

front: Patient over 50 with cardiovascular risk factors and accelerated HTN?

items.a: Renal artery stenosis from atherosclerosis.
Renal artery stenosis from atherosclerosis.

front: Heart failure patient with low O2 sats who refuses to lie back?

items.a: Furosemide. CXR or exam may show fluid 2/3 up the lung fields. Do not confuse with ACEi/ARB: those are first line to increase EF in heart failure even if O2 sats are low (decrease AT-II constriction, decrease afterload), but loops are first-line if the vignette emphasizes dyspnea and low O2 sats.

front: Healthy 70-year-old versus 20-year-old lung volumes?

front: Watery diarrhea in an immunocompromised patient?

items.a: Cryptosporidium parvum.

front: HIV patient with lobar pneumonia: PJP or S. pneumoniae?

items.a: S. pneumoniae (continues on p420). PJP gives bilateral interstitial infiltrates with a ground-glass appearance; S. pneumoniae is lobar.

front: Upper lobe nodular density in an immunocompromised patient?

items.a: Aspergilloma.

front: 13F with irregular periods: next step?

items.a: Reexamine in one year (reassurance); periods are typically abnormal in the first year after menarche.

front: 13F never had a period, suprapubic mass, nausea and vomiting?

items.a: Beta-hCG: she is pregnant. Girls can get pregnant before ever having a period; must rule out.

front: 14F with a massive unilateral breast mass, sister died of breast cancer?

items.a: Follow up in six months: virginal breast hypertrophy is normal in puberty.

front: 15M with unilateral mass behind the nipple +/- tenderness?

items.a: Reassurance: physiologic gynecomastia of puberty (higher androgens aromatized to estrogens).

front: 17F with severe period pain and normal exam?

items.a: Primary dysmenorrhea from prostaglandin hypersecretion (PGF2alpha); give NSAIDs.

front: 23F with severe period pain + nodular uterosacral ligaments?

items.a: Endometriosis: diagnostic laparoscopy.

front: 14M at 3rd percentile for height + bone age less than chronologic age?

items.a: Constitutional short stature (he will catch up; growth curve shifted right).

front: 14M at 3rd percentile for height: next step in diagnosis?

items.a: Ask about the parents' height trajectory; if the stem says parents are average height, do a bone age.

front: 16F Tanner stage II + wide neck + bone age equal to chronologic age?

items.a: Turner syndrome: genuine short stature (e.g., 4'11"), Tanner I-II, cystic hygroma (lymphatic insufficiency; wide/webbed neck).

front: Adult male 4 feet tall with large head and trunk relative to limbs?

items.a: Achondroplasia.

front: Adult male 4 feet tall with head and trunk proportional to limbs?

items.a: Laron dwarfism (growth hormone receptor defect, GH insensitivity).

front: 42M two days after surgery: restlessness, tremulousness, tachycardia, diaphoresis?

items.a: Delirium tremens (alcohol withdrawal).
Delirium tremens (alcohol withdrawal).

front: 42M two days after surgery: restlessness + tactile/visual hallucinations?

items.a: Alcoholic hallucinosis (same spectrum as DT); treat with a long-acting benzodiazepine.

front: 22F BP 160/110, FMD confirmed on MR angiography, normal electrolytes and pH: AT-II and aldosterone?

items.a: Both high. The source says biochemistry can be completely normal in aldosterone derangement; if the stem insists on a confirmed cause of hyperaldosteronism with high BP, AT-II and aldosterone are both high.

front: Child with a heart tumor?

items.a: Cardiac rhabdomyoma until proven otherwise.

front: 2-year-old with cardiac myxoma + perioral melanosis + hyperthyroidism?

items.a: Carney complex: cardiac myxoma + perioral melanosis + endocrine hypersecretion (classically bilateral pigmented zona fasciculata hyperplasia causing Cushing; can be hyperthyroidism or growth hormone).

front: 32F with pedal and forearm edema after starting an antihypertensive?

items.a: Fluid retention from a dihydropyridine CCB (e.g., nifedipine), a really HY side effect.

front: Diabetic patient on HCTZ for HTN?

items.a: Stop the thiazide and use an ACEi or ARB.

front: Delirium in a patient on a thiazide?

items.a: Think hypercalcemia (high Ca is a HY USMLE cause of CNS dysfunction, 'hypercalcemic crisis').

front: 28F non-smoker with loud P2 + RVH?

items.a: Primary pulmonary hypertension.

front: Kid given an OTC cold medicine, then mental status changes?

items.a: Anticholinergic delirium from a first-generation antihistamine (diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine).

front: 22M takes a drug, nystagmus + bellicosity?

items.a: PCP.

front: 22M takes a drug, mutism + constricted pupils?

items.a: PCP (the source says it is on the psych NBME for 2CK; I did not verify).

front: 2-year-old holding his sister's hand falls, holds arm pronated at his side?

items.a: Nursemaid's elbow (radial head subluxation).

front: Kid falls on outstretched arm + anatomical snuffbox pain?

items.a: Scaphoid fracture; next best step is x-ray (continues on p425 if x-ray is negative).

front: Golden crusty lesions around the mouth in a school-age child?

items.a: Impetigo, not HSV.

front: 32F with a sharply demarcated fiery red lesion from knee to ankle + fever 101F?

items.a: Erysipelas: infection of the superficial dermis +/- dermal lymphatics (cellulitis is the hypodermis); the superficial depth gives a well-demarcated fiery look, while cellulitis is more diffuse and pink.

front: Perineal gangrene in a 50M diabetic?

items.a: Fournier gangrene: surgical debridement.

front: 17M with worsening cellulitis holding an amoxicillin canister from his GP?

items.a: Improper antibiotic: he should have had oral dicloxacillin or oral cephalexin; the cellulitis must be Staph, not Strep.

front: 72M left facial droop + left arm and leg weakness with hyperreflexia + left Babinski + intact sensation?

items.a: Lacunar infarct of the internal capsule: 'pure motor' stroke (posterior limb); thalamic stroke gives 'pure sensory'. Lacunar infarcts usually follow hypertension causing lipohyalinosis of lenticulostriate arteries.

front: 6F finds an open aspirin bottle: finding best suggesting a toxic dose?

items.a: Increased respiratory rate: acute respiratory alkalosis (respiratory center upregulation; high pH, low CO2, no bicarb change). After roughly 20 minutes a mixed metabolic acidosis-respiratory alkalosis (low pH, low CO2, low bicarb); the low bicarb is not compensation, since salicylic acid itself is an acid. Tachypnea is the first observed sign (continues on p428).

front: 30M with shooting groin pain + high BP + mother had thyroid cancer surgery: best test?

items.a: Urinary metanephrines. Diagnosis MEN 2A: pheochromocytoma + medullary thyroid carcinoma + primary hyperparathyroidism. Treat pheo with phenoxybenzamine (irreversible alpha blocker); groin pain is urolithiasis from hypercalcemia; medullary thyroid cancer raises calcitonin. MEN I: pancreatic tumor, pituitary tumor, primary hyperparathyroidism. MEN 2B: pheochromocytoma + medullary thyroid carcinoma + mucosal neuromas + Marfanoid habitus.

front: Neonate with a hereditary disease and homozygous gene deletion: inheritance pattern?

items.a: Autosomal recessive: 'homozygous deletion' with no mention of parental disease implies it.

front: 84F with unilateral hydronephrosis from ureteral compression by a vascular structure?

items.a: The ipsilateral common iliac artery. If the stem says cancer causes unilateral hydronephrosis: ovarian cancer; bilateral hydronephrosis from cancer: cervical cancer (usually younger).

front: 54M dyspnea 4 months + ascites + leg edema + bilateral pleural effusions + EF 55%: mechanism of lung fluid?

items.a: Decreased plasma colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure (nephrotic syndrome or hepatic disease with low albumin). Wrong answer: increased capillary hydrostatic pressure (left heart failure, but EF is normal). Increased vascular permeability is for ARDS, pneumonia/sepsis, or PE (continues on p429).

front: Neonate with persistent cyanosis, normal Hct and RBC morphology, normal CXR and echo?

items.a: Methemoglobinemia from cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency (congenital). Inhaled nitric oxide for neonatal pulmonary hypertension can cause it (oxidizes ferrous to ferric iron). Acrocyanosis is a normal bluish tinge of the extremities (treat with warming lights and tactile stimulation). Treatment in most cases: methylene blue + vitamin C.

front: 40F with fibromuscular dysplasia and normal GFR: explanation?

items.a: Increased efferent arteriolar resistance: RAAS upregulates, angiotensin II constricts efferent arterioles, raising filtration fraction so GFR is held despite lower renal blood flow.

front: 19F with external compression of the left renal artery but normal renal perfusion pressure?

items.a: Decreased afferent arteriolar resistance (the source's answer in this hypothetical; afferent arterioles distal to the compression dilate). The source notes the usual response to reduced perfusion is efferent constriction via RAAS, which maintains GFR rather than perfusion.

front: 27M from Pennsylvania, splenectomy, intraerythrocytic rings?

items.a: Babesia: malaria-like hemolytic disorder in people who have never left the United States; ring forms and Maltese crosses in RBCs (continues on p430).

front: 2F with a missing superior left parathyroid gland: embryologic defect?

items.a: Fourth pharyngeal pouch (superior parathyroids; third pouch = thymus + inferior parathyroids). Pouches are endoderm, arches mesoderm, clefts/grooves ectoderm. DiGeorge: aplasia of the 3rd and 4th pouches with hypocalcemia, T cell deficiency (absent thymic shadow), cleft lip/palate, heart defects (tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus).

front: 20F recurrent Staph infections + CD18 deficiency?

items.a: Failure of phagocyte emigration to inflamed tissue: leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LFA-1/CD18 integrin needed for diapedesis); recurrent infections (often Staph) with absent pus; delayed umbilical cord separation is often omitted as too easy.

front: 40F develops AML after an exposure: likely agent?

items.a: Benzene. Naphthylamine is associated with urothelial cancers; vinyl chloride with hepatic angiosarcoma.

front: 35F on high-dose vitamins: cracked lips, rough dry skin, scalp alopecia?

items.a: Excess vitamin A: desquamation, increased transaminases, dyslipidemia, pseudotumor cerebri; teratogenic (pregnancy test before isotretinoin for acne).

front: 46M alcoholic with hypersegmented neutrophils?

items.a: Folate (B9) deficiency, the most common vitamin deficiency; also tea-and-toast diet and antiepileptics (valproate, phenytoin, carbamazepine). B12 is for veganism/strict vegetarianism, chronic gastritis, pernicious anemia, gastrectomy or ileectomy, Crohn, D. latum.

front: 34F receives phentolamine: intracellular effect?

items.a: Decreased phospholipase C activity: phentolamine is an alpha-1 antagonist; alpha-1 is Gq-coupled (agonism raises PLC, IP3, DAG; antagonism lowers them, continues on p432).

front: 17F heavy menses + easy bruising + low Hb + normal platelets + normal PT + increased PTT: deficient factor?

items.a: von Willebrand factor: bridges Gp Ib on platelets to endothelium. Bleeding time always increased; PT normal; PTT increased only about half the time (stabilizing factor VIII is a secondary role); many NBME items have a normal PTT. Platelets normal or slightly low.

front: 43M elevated fasting glucose + arthritis + cardiomegaly: mechanism?

items.a: Increased intestinal iron absorption: hemochromatosis (AR, chromosome 6). Iron deposits in the pancreas tail (diabetes), heart (dilated or restrictive cardiomyopathy), hypothalamus/testes (infertility), skin ('bronze diabetes'). Hemochromatosis and primary hyperparathyroidism are two HY causes of pseudogout (CPPD), which can mimic OA even with Heberden nodes. Next step: check serum iron and ferritin.

front: 6M with perioral hyperpigmentation + colonic polyps?

items.a: Hamartomatous polyps: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (perioral melanosis + hamartomatous polyps).

front: 26F hyperpigmentation + BP 100/60 + muscle weakness: sodium, potassium, cortisol?

items.a: Low sodium, high potassium, low cortisol: Addison disease (aldosterone is low). Often autoantibodies against 21-hydroxylase, needed for both aldosterone and cortisol synthesis.

front: 40F on chemotherapy with a low leukocyte count: helpful drug?

items.a: Pegfilgrastim (G-CSF), which increases neutrophils.

front: 27M infertile with high testosterone and low LH/FSH?

items.a: Exogenous testosterone use (a testosterone-secreting tumor could theoretically be an answer, but only the former is listed).

front: 46M with esophageal varices: vein with increased flow?

items.a: Left gastric vein: increased portal venous pressure backs up into the left gastric vein, then esophageal veins.

front: 74M cheek lesion with neoplastic cells with dense pigment granules?

items.a: Melanoma (the source says it sounds like pigmented BCC, but USMLE wants melanoma). BCC: islands and nests of basophilic cells; SCC: keratin pearls and intercellular bridges.

front: 50F weight loss + dyspnea + pleural-based mass encasing the lungs: cell of origin?

items.a: Mesothelial cells (mesothelioma): classically pleural/supradiaphragmatic plaques; grossly it surrounds the lungs circumferentially rather than forming an isolated mass.

front: 30F LMP 8 weeks ago, no fetus or sac on ultrasound, curettage shows trophoblastic proliferation: chromosomes?

items.a: 46,XX: complete mole (an empty egg fertilized by one sperm that duplicates; only paternal genetic material; no fetal parts). Partial mole: one egg fertilized by two sperm, fetal parts present on ultrasound; the source gives a '67 chromosome' karyotype (a typical partial mole is triploid, 69 chromosomes; I did not verify the source figure).

front: 35F menorrhagia + hoarse voice + delayed reflexes + globular heart + low Hct and MCV: next step?

items.a: Check serum TSH: probable Hashimoto hypothyroidism (menorrhagia, slow reflexes, cardiomyopathy). Anemia is likely iron deficiency from heavy periods (though anemia of chronic disease also shows low MCV on many NBME items). Other HY: hypothyroid myopathy (increased CK), raised LDL, raised transaminases, low mood; constipation, cold intolerance, brittle hair, doughy skin are often omitted as too easy.

front: 25M with 3 days of leg paresthesias + dysphagia + diminished reflexes, CSF protein 70 mg/dL with 5 cells/uL?

items.a: Guillain-Barre syndrome: 'destruction of myelin and endoneurial lymphocytic infiltrates'; CSF albuminocytologic dissociation (high protein, normal cells).

front: 25M with palm and sole rash, given a previously received antibiotic, now fever, tachycardia, tachypnea?

items.a: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (reaction to lysis of spirochetes) in secondary syphilis (palms/soles rash) treated with penicillin G.

front: 30F with RA on infliximab who has not improved: likely mediator?

items.a: IL-1. Infliximab is a monoclonal antibody against soluble TNF-alpha (not the receptor), so TNF-alpha is not the answer; IL-1 and IL-6 drive RA inflammation; tocilizumab is an anti-IL-6 receptor monoclonal antibody for advanced RA.

front: 20M with both common carotids externally compressed for 10 seconds: effects?

items.a: Alveolar ventilation, venous tone, arterial tone, and blood pressure all increase. Less carotid sinus flow lowers baroreceptor stretch and CN IX afferent firing to the solitary nucleus; vagal efferent firing falls and sympathetic efferent firing rises (increasing heart rate), with alpha-1 vasoconstriction (more SVR, more BP) and beta-2 bronchodilation and higher respiratory rate.

front: 39M bilateral renal enlargement + high BP + father died of subarachnoid hemorrhage: mutated protein?

items.a: Polycystin (ADPKD); hypertension from cysts compressing renal microvasculature causing RAAS surges.

front: 52M with 3 months of esophageal burning, diabetes, reduced pin-prick to the ankles, HbA1c 9.6%: MOA of best drug?

items.a: D2 receptor antagonism: metoclopramide for diabetic gastroparesis (prokinetic and antiemetic). With a plain GERD-like picture and no poor diabetic control: trial of PPI or H2 blocker (if forced to choose, PPI).

front: 30F cuts a finger and bleeding stops quickly: mechanism?

items.a: Localized secretion of endothelin (it acts peripherally as well as in pulmonary vascular resistance).

front: 28M with renal failure + hematuria + hearing loss?

items.a: Alport syndrome: type IV collagen mutation (X-linked). Wrong answer: antibodies against type IV collagen (Goodpasture). Alport: male with hematuria + ear and/or eye problem; Goodpasture: male in his 20s-40s with hematuria and hemoptysis.

front: 19F with alkaline urine and renal calculi: organism?

items.a: Proteus (Klebsiella or Serratia could also be correct): struvite (ammonium magnesium phosphate) stones form in alkaline urine from UTIs by urease-positive organisms.

front: 62F high Hb, WBCs, platelets, pO2 93%: EPO and arterial O2 content?

items.a: Low EPO + normal arterial O2 content: polycythemia vera (JAK2 mutation), marrow overproduction suppresses renal EPO; WBCs and/or platelets also high. In secondary polycythemia (lung disease: high EPO from low O2; renal cell carcinoma: tumor EPO) only RBCs are high. Treatment of PV: serial phlebotomy.

front: Newborn with chorioretinitis + cataracts + microcephaly and no other info?

items.a: CMV. Congenital toxoplasmosis is always the triad chorioretinitis + hydrocephalus + intracranial calcifications; without that triad, eliminate it. Congenital CMV has nonspecific findings (deafness, chorioretinitis, intracranial calcifications). Congenital rubella: PDA; congenital syphilis: Hutchinson teeth, often saddle nose and/or saber shins (continues on p440 for VZV).

front: 14M temp 103F + WBC 25,000 with neutrophil shift: mechanism?

items.a: Accelerated release of leukocytes from the bone marrow postmitotic reserve pool: leukemoid reaction (leukocytosis with infection); leukocyte ALP is high.

front: 15M skiing accident, tachycardia, tachypnea, BP 98/72, decreased right breath sounds, black pleural space on CXR?

items.a: Tension pneumothorax: hemodynamic decompensation (BP may be low-normal only because the heart rate compensates). Low BP comes from compressed venous return to the right atrium. Tracheal deviation need not be mentioned. Treatment: needle decompression then chest tube to an underwater seal.

front: 36M stab wound to chest + low BP + JVD + systolic BP drops 12 mmHg on inspiration?

items.a: Cardiac tamponade: Beck triad (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds; not all need be mentioned). Pulsus paradoxus is a systolic drop >10 mmHg on inspiration. Tamponade is a pericardial effusion plus hemodynamic decompensation; ECG shows electrical alternans (also seen in a simple effusion; continues on p441).

front: 42F in hospital 2 days after surgery, short of breath, HR 92, normal ECG: MOA of the needed drug?

items.a: Activation of antithrombin (heparin) for pulmonary embolism. Sinus tachycardia is the most common ECG finding. After heparin, spiral CT of the chest; V/Q scan first in pregnant women.

front: 29M with spontaneous lancinating cheek pain lasting seconds: location of the problem?

items.a: Pons (CN V arises there); can also be 'microvascular compression of CN V': trigeminal neuralgia. No acute treatment since it subsides quickly; prophylaxis is carbamazepine.

front: 50M severe upper back pain + holodiastolic murmur loudest after S2?

items.a: Aortic dissection: pain between the scapulae; retrograde dissection can dilate the aortic root causing aortic regurgitation (decrescendo holodiastolic murmur); CXR widened mediastinum; give labetalol to reduce shearing forces. Risk: Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos; greatest risks hypertension and cocaine.

front: 19M chest pain after heavy partying, walks in bent over at the waist: next step in diagnosis?

items.a: ECG showing diffuse ST elevations: pericarditis. Pain eases leaning forward and worsens leaning back; ST elevation in most leads (vs 3-4 contiguous leads in MI); cocaine is a risk factor for serous pericarditis. Treatment: NSAIDs, corticosteroids, colchicine.

front: 37F with RA, PR depressions and ST elevations in many leads?

items.a: Pericarditis: common in autoimmune disease; PR depression is highly specific but uncommon; diffuse ST elevation is present in all USMLE cases that mention ECG findings.

front: 34F with severe chest pain worse reaching behind her back and above her head?

items.a: Costochondritis: MSK because it changes with position (pericarditis is the only cardiac exception).

front: 40M with alcoholism, K 3.2, still 3.2 after potassium?

items.a: Hypomagnesemia: check serum Mg for low Ca and K that do not respond to supplementation. Mg is needed for basal PTH secretion (low Mg, low Ca) and inhibits a distal renal K secretory pump (low Mg, K wasting). Alcoholics are at risk from dietary deficiency (ethanol is 7 kcal/g).

front: 18M lost hiking for 3 weeks, BMI 27: electrolyte worry on refeeding?

items.a: Hypophosphatemia (refeeding syndrome): rapid sequestration of phosphate by glycolytic intermediates as glycolysis resumes.

front: 31F with ITP, splenectomy, platelets normalize, low again 6 months later?

items.a: Accessory spleen (about 10% of people have one, <1 cm; it can grow after splenectomy).

front: 49M with long alcoholism, smelly stools, normal pancreatic enzymes?

items.a: Chronic pancreatitis: exocrine insufficiency from repeated acute bouts; enzymes low or low-normal; steatorrhea from lack of lipase; treat with pancrelipase.

front: 49M recovered from pancreatitis a week ago, now fever + leukocytosis + high lipase and amylase?

items.a: Pseudocyst (no true walls; pancreatic parenchyma encases the fluid); can be drained internally via ERCP (2CK surgery NBME, per the source).

front: 40F found hypothermic, rewarmed, red feet: electrolyte worry?

items.a: Hyperkalemia: reperfusion injury oxygen radicals raise the risk of rhabdomyolysis, especially in alcoholics.

front: 82F found by the stairs, urine blood 2+, 3-4 RBCs/hpf?

items.a: Rhabdomyolysis: false-positive urine dipstick blood; USMLE can give 3-4 RBCs/hpf as the false positive.

front: 44M after surgery with tachycardia, fever, high BP: drug?

items.a: Chlordiazepoxide (benzodiazepine) for delirium tremens; the tremor of DT is explained by beta-2 agonism (source).

front: 57F comatose + seizure + prolonged QRS on ECG?

items.a: Amitriptyline (TCA toxicity: coma, convulsions, cardiotoxicity). Treat with sodium bicarbonate, which decreases TCA binding to myocardial sodium channels. The source says urinary alkalinization for excretion is the wrong rationale (that refers to salicylates; TCAs are basic).

front: 22M on an antidepressant with suprapubic mass and hot red face?

items.a: A TCA (e.g., amitriptyline): anticholinergic effects, opposite of DUMBBELSS: constipation, urinary retention, mydriasis, tachycardia, relaxed skeletal muscle tone, dry eyes, dry mouth, anhidrosis (heat retention, red hot patient).

front: 30F given diphenhydramine for motion sickness: receptor responsible?

items.a: Antimuscarinic: first-generation H1 blockers (diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine) have anticholinergic effects; muscarinic blockade eases motion sickness. They do not act on H2.

front: 24M cuts his arm: cell that decreases infection risk in the acute setting?

items.a: Neutrophils: acute inflammation, innate immunity; phagocytose and kill bacteria via lysosomal hydrolases and H2O2 (continues on p445).

front: 55M with hyperthyroidism and absent left leg pulses?

items.a: Arterial embolic occlusion: left atrial mural thrombus from hyperthyroidism-induced atrial fibrillation lodging in the femoral artery. In DVT pulses are normal. AF emboli can also cause stroke or acute mesenteric ischemia (SMA/IMA).

front: 80M with atrial fibrillation + severe abdominal pain + mild tenderness?

items.a: Acute mesenteric ischemia: pain out of proportion to exam; embolus to SMA or IMA from left atrial thrombus.

front: 65M with diabetes, prior CABG, claudication, abdominal pain 1-2 hours after meals?

items.a: Chronic mesenteric ischemia from atherosclerosis. It sounds like a duodenal ulcer, but the patient has a severe cardiovascular history; H. pylori ulcer is usually a younger immigrant patient.

front: 30M with RA overdoses on methotrexate, massive hepatonecrosis: liver regeneration mechanism?

items.a: Recruitment of cells from G0 into the cell cycle (quiescent hepatocytes enter G1). Wrong answer: stem cells entering G1.

front: 20F with an insulinoma: C-peptide, insulin, ketones?

items.a: High C-peptide, high insulin, low ketones. C-peptide is cleaved off during endogenous insulin production; insulin inhibits ketogenesis; beta-oxidation is inhibited by malonyl-CoA from insulin-stimulated fatty acid synthesis.

front: 2M with anemia, erythroblasts with ferritin granules, decreased delta-ALA synthase: vitamin?

items.a: Vitamin B6: X-linked sideroblastic anemia. Heme synthesis starts with succinyl-CoA + glycine by delta-ALA synthase (needs B6). Sideroblastic anemia can be X-linked or classically alcohol-related; Prussian blue shows ringed sideroblasts (iron stuck around mitochondria in RBC precursors).

front: 62F flank mass + calcium 11.5 + hemoglobin 18.5?

items.a: Paraneoplastic syndrome from renal cell carcinoma: PTHrP (hypercalcemia) and EPO (high Hb); continues on p447.

front: MR patient with symptoms of heart failure or ischemia before surgery?

items.a: Do a pre-op stress test to determine MI risk (unlike mere MR without symptoms or other risk factors).

front: 45M with nosebleeds since adolescence, S3, dyspnea, red dots on the tongue?

items.a: Cause of dyspnea: pulmonary arteriovenous fistula (high-output failure); diagnosis hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. Stems usually show red dots on the tongue, mouth, or finger.

front: Spirometry curve in a 34-year-old with no family history and a 5-year smoking history?

items.a: Concave (obstructive) curve: choose asthma over COPD as most likely in this patient (per the source's reasoning).

front: Edema in a patient on an NSAID?

items.a: Cause: decreased renal sodium excretion (PCT sodium reabsorption increased, FENa <1%). Management: discontinue ibuprofen.

front: 28-year-old with LLQ cramping and bloody diarrhea 7 days after oral antibiotics?

items.a: C. difficile (wrong answer Yersinia). Any antibiotic can cause it. Diagnose with stool AB toxin test, not culture. Treat with oral vancomycin (stays in the GI tract). The source says it has never seen fidaxomicin or rifaximin on NBME.

front: Euthyroid or hypothyroid patient with a thyroid nodule: ultrasound or FNA?

items.a: The source's conclusion from NBME/Free 120: ultrasound is correct over FNA if both are listed; if ultrasound is not listed, choose FNA. First palpate the gland, then check TSH.

front: 42M with 3 years of GERD + CXR air-fluid level behind the cardiac silhouette?

items.a: Hiatal hernia (next steps on p267).

front: 42M with hiatal hernia: next best step in diagnosis?

items.a: Barium swallow, which shows the proximal stomach herniating through the esophageal hiatus.

front: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal enzymes + autoimmune disease in the patient or family?

items.a: Primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC).

front: 8-day-old neonate with jaundice, direct bilirubin 14, total 15 mg/dL?

items.a: Biliary atresia (super HY). Next best step in diagnosis per the source: straight to liver biopsy; if positive, liver transplant.

front: 79M with atrial fibrillation + severe acute diffuse abdominal pain?

items.a: Acute mesenteric ischemia from a mural thrombus embolizing to the SMA or IMA. Next step in management: mesenteric arteriography.

front: Treatment of the 79M with acute mesenteric ischemia?

items.a: Antibiotics (for necrotic bowel) then laparotomy to remove necrotic bowel. The source says the stem states IV antibiotics were given and asks the next step: laparotomy. USMLE wants resection of nonviable bowel, though the literature mentions embolectomy.

front: 52F with a short ventricular fibrillation episode, defibrillated, now severe abdominal pain?

items.a: Acute mesenteric ischemia from ischemia due to VF, not an embolus: antibiotics; CT if stable; if unstable go straight to laparotomy.

front: 55F diabetic with claudication + abdominal pain 1-2 hours after meals?

items.a: Chronic mesenteric ischemia from severe atherosclerosis of the SMA or IMA (angina of the bowel).

front: Chronic mesenteric ischemia patient with 2 days of severe abdominal pain and fever?

items.a: Acute on chronic mesenteric ischemia (thrombosis; an 'MI' of the bowel): mesenteric arteriography to diagnose; antibiotics + laparotomy to remove necrotic bowel.

front: 87F with a coffee bean sign on AXR and obstipation?

items.a: Sigmoid volvulus; the source says the surgery NBME treatment is sigmoidoscopy-guided placement of a rectal tube.

front: 22M stressed studying, yellow eyes, similar past episodes, otherwise healthy?

items.a: Gilbert syndrome (decreased glucuronosyltransferase expression, the bilirubin-conjugating enzyme; reduced ability to take up unconjugated bilirubin at the liver). Treatment is reassurance; it is benign.

front: 16F with fever, leukocytosis, RLQ pain migrating from the epigastrium?

items.a: Appendicitis. Epigastric pain is visceral; RLQ pain is parietal peritoneal inflammation. In females, pregnancy test + adnexal ultrasound for gyn causes (e.g., ruptured cyst); in males go straight to laparoscopy; if gyn causes are ruled out, laparoscopic removal.

front: 2-week-old male with forceful non-bilious vomiting?

items.a: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Diagnose with abdominal ultrasound showing an olive-shaped hypertrophied pylorus.

front: 2-week-old male with bilious vomiting?

items.a: Duodenal atresia, annular pancreas, congenital midgut volvulus, or Hirschsprung (Hirschsprung can present with bilious vomiting).

front: 2-week-old with Down syndrome + bilious vomiting + passed meconium vs slow to pass meconium?

items.a: Passed meconium: duodenal atresia. Slow to pass meconium: Hirschsprung.

front: 18-month-old with intermittent abdominal pain, crying, blood in stool?

items.a: Intussusception (the same for intermittent squatting or legs to chest + vomiting + FOBT positive).

front: 18-month-old with legs to chest, vomiting, FOBT negative?

items.a: Congenital midgut volvulus (it sounds like intussusception but there is no blood per rectum).

front: 45M cirrhosis + fluid wave + fever + abdominal pain?

items.a: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). Same for a diabetic on peritoneal dialysis with fever and abdominal pain, and for a child with minimal change disease causing ascites.

front: Woman in her 20s-50s with high cholesterol, diffuse pruritus, sister with rheumatoid arthritis?

items.a: Primary biliary cirrhosis (autoimmune diseases go together in patient or family). Dx: anti-mitochondrial Abs first; liver biopsy confirms.

front: Neonate born at 32 weeks with fever, abdominal distension, feeding intolerance, hematochezia?

items.a: Necrotizing enterocolitis, bowel infection in premature neonates, usually <32 weeks gestation.

front: 49M with abdominal pain after meals, now sepsis + diffuse acute abdominal pain?

items.a: Ruptured viscus (duodenum). Next step: x-ray of chest + abdomen to look for air under the diaphragm. The source says the exam gives CXR alone, AXR alone, or both as choices.

front: 42M with dysphagia to solids and liquids from the start?

items.a: Achalasia. Inability to swallow solids and liquids together implies a neurogenic cause.

front: 42M with EtOH history and dysphagia to solids that progresses to liquids?

items.a: Esophageal cancer (SCC). Dysphagia to solids progressing to solids + liquids is cancer until proven otherwise.

front: 42M overweight with halitosis, gurgling with fluids, regurgitating undigested food?

items.a: Next step: barium (or gastrografin) swallow; Dx = Zenker diverticulum. With a GERD history, go straight to endoscopy (cancer, not Zenker).

front: 52F with 2 kids, BMI 28, recurrent colicky epigastric pain?

items.a: Ultrasound (cholelithiasis).

front: 45F BMI 29, BP 140/90, high TG, low HDL, high fasting glucose, mildly high AST/ALT?

items.a: NASH from metabolic syndrome; treat with lifestyle modification. The source adds that stems may show completely normal labs, leaving 'she has metabolic syndrome' as the clue.

front: 69M with LLQ pain + fever?

items.a: Diverticulitis. CT abdomen with contrast; antibiotics (metronidazole PLUS a fluoroquinolone or Augmentin; metronidazole covers anaerobes). Never scope during suspected diverticulitis (perforation); colonoscopy after it is cleared to rule out malignancy.

front: 25M with oral ulcer + bloody diarrhea?

items.a: Crohn disease.

front: 28M with morning-worse low back pain that improves through the day + mouth ulcer?

items.a: Crohn disease (oral involvement) + sacroiliitis (ankylosing spondylitis back pain).

front: 20F with bloody diarrhea, sore joints, eczematoid plaque on forehead?

items.a: IBD + psoriatic arthritis.

front: 65M with intermittent bloody diarrhea, now 104F fever, abdominal pain, high WBC?

items.a: Toxic megacolon. Dx with AXR (dilated bowel, e.g., 12-cm cecum), not colonoscopy (perforation). AXR is done when looking for gas.

front: 55M BMI 33, no diabetes mentioned, 3 months burning in throat?

items.a: GERD; treat with a 2-week PPI trial (omeprazole); relief supports GERD.

front: 55M BMI 33, poorly controlled diabetes, 3 months burning in throat?

items.a: Diabetic gastroparesis, not GERD. First pharmacologic treatment metoclopramide; if not listed, erythromycin (motilin receptor agonist).

front: Gynecomastia in a male with an NBME answer of Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor?

items.a: SL tumors make androgens; gynecomastia is possible because of aromatization of androgens to estrogens (granulosa cell tumor not listed).

front: Gynecomastia in a male taking hCG?

items.a: Mechanism: testis producing estrogen. hCG acts like LH + FSH: LH drives androgens, FSH drives aromatase, so androgens convert to estrogens.

front: 13-year-old who never had a period with nausea, bloating, breast tenderness?

items.a: Check serum beta-hCG (pregnancy can occur before first menses). Always check beta-hCG before isotretinoin (teratogenic).

front: Mini-summary of male differentiation?

items.a: SRY/TDF forms testes; MIF from Sertoli cells regresses Mullerian ducts; testosterone from Leydig cells promotes Wolffian ducts.

front: Male-female equivalents?

items.a: Labioscrotal swelling: scrotum/labia majora. Urogenital folds: ventral penile shaft and urethra/labia minora. Urogenital sinus: prostate/Skene glands; Cowper glands/Bartholin glands. Genital tubercle: corpora/vestibular bulbs; glans penis/glans clitoris.

front: Child with foul-smelling vaginal discharge and no trauma?

items.a: Vaginal foreign body (children or elderly; no lacerations means not abuse). Sexual abuse vignettes mention lacerations, with or without discharge.

front: First event before female puberty?

items.a: Breast bud development.

front: CAH mechanism in a 46,XX girl with fused labia?

items.a: ACTH hypersecretion: low cortisol raises ACTH, driving adrenal androgens (DHEA-S).

front: Neonate of a diabetic mother?

items.a: Maternal insulin does not cross the placenta; the fetus makes its own and stays hyperinsulinemic after birth, causing hypoglycemia (rigors, seizure; answer: decreased gluconeogenesis). Possible pentad: hypoglycemia, hyperbilirubinemia, polycythemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia. Long QT: choose hypocalcemia over hypomagnesemia.

front: Thyroid labs in a euthyroid pregnant woman?

items.a: Normal TSH, normal free T4, increased total T4 (estrogen increases TBG; the source says estrogen, not progesterone).

front: Postmenopausal overweight woman with bleeding?

items.a: Endometrial biopsy; past anovulatory cycles and hyperplasia increase endometrial cancer risk.

front: Male differentiation cascade?

items.a: SRY gives testis-determining factor, so testes form (90% seminiferous tubules). Leydig cells make testosterone (Wolffian structures), converted to DHT by 5-alpha-reductase (prostate and external male structures).

front: 18F with no withdrawal bleeding?

items.a: Untreated for ten years: osteoporosis (low estrogen).

front: 42F with heavy painful periods?

items.a: Two kids, no more wanted, husband to have vasectomy, regular periods, no other abnormalities: endometrial ablation.

front: Large breast lump in a 14-year-old?

items.a: 4x6 cm slightly tender left breast mass, aunt died of breast cancer: follow up in 6 months (virginal breast hypertrophy, a normal response to estrogen).

front: 13F with no menses, morning vomiting and suprapubic fullness?

items.a: Beta-hCG (pregnancy can occur before first menstruation).

front: 32F infertile 3 years with BMI 30 and acanthosis?

items.a: Type 2 diabetes (PCOS/anovulation not listed; hypercortisolism wrong since no striae, wasting or central obesity).

front: 46,XX neonate with phallus and scrotum?

items.a: Mechanism: ACTH hypersecretion (21- or 11-hydroxylase deficiency lowers cortisol; precursors shunt to DHEA-S and androstenedione, virilizing).

front: 21F requesting OCPs?

items.a: Pap normal: also check for chlamydia (Pap starts at 21, STI checks from sexual onset).

front: Child with discharge and spotting?

items.a: 5F foul yellow discharge, spotting, mild vulvar erythema: vaginal foreign body (abuse would show lacerations or trauma). 82F with Alzheimer and 3 cm laceration, edematous perineal body: sexual assault.

front: G3P2 Rh-negative at first visit?

items.a: Received RhoGAM before: indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) test to see whether she formed anti-Rh antibodies.

front: Neonate with PDA?

items.a: Mother may have had arthritis, not rash: congenital rubella.

front: Hepatitis B and the newborn?

items.a: Mother HBsAg positive: HBIG + vaccine within 12 hours. Negative: vaccine within 12 hours. Unknown: vaccine within 12 hours, HBIG within 7 days if her test is positive or stays unknown.

front: 16F, 5 feet 9 inches, sparse hair?

items.a: AIS (karyotypically male despite 'girl' in the stem).

front: 12F with clitoromegaly and no uterus?

items.a: One-year hair growth and acne, 2 cm vaginal canal, clitoromegaly, posterior labioscrotal fusion, no cervix or uterus: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency; shelf asks karyotype: 46,XY.

front: Prior 4540 g neonate?

items.a: Increased risk of gestational diabetes. Screen normal-risk women at 24-28 weeks.

front: Diabetic mother's neonate with NRDS?

items.a: Fetal hormone responsible: insulin (inhibits surfactant production); maternal insulin does not cross the placenta.
